query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy, the synergistic action of wear and corrosion is driven by micro-galvanic coupling between dissimilar eutectic phases. Mechanical wear at elevated temperatures continuously removes or thins protective oxide layers on the more corrosion‐resistant phase, thereby exposing the adjacent, less noble phase to accelerated localized corrosion. As this corrosion further weakens the phase boundaries and interfacial regions, the wear process is enhanced, leading to an overall accelerated coupled degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinct phases that have different electrochemical potentials and pre-formed protective oxide films on at least one phase.
generation.intervention: Simultaneous exposure of the alloy to mechanical wear and a corrosive environment at elevated temperature.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., 450 °C to 650 °C) under conditions where both mechanical wear (abrasion or sliding contact) and corrosive attack (acidic or molten salt environment) are present concurrently.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfaces between dissimilar phases, where differences in nobility lead to galvanic cells, and the integrity of the protective oxide films.
generation.mechanism: Wear removes protective oxide layers on the more noble phase, exposing the adjacent less corrosion-resistant phase. The resulting micro-galvanic coupling accelerates localized corrosion along phase boundaries. Corrosion-induced weakening of these interfaces further facilitates mechanical material removal, creating a positive feedback loop of accelerated degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline conditions (individual wear or corrosion tests), the simultaneous action yields a higher total degradation rate. Specifically, both the wear rate (depth or material loss) and corrosion rate (pitting or selective dissolution) are predicted to increase synergistically beyond simple additive effects.
generation.baseline: Degradation measured under isolated wear conditions (with an intact oxide film) or under static corrosion conditions (where oxide layers remain relatively undisturbed) at the same temperature.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is assumed to be active in eutectic HEAs with microstructures exhibiting phase contrast in electrochemical behavior and in environments where the oxide film is mechanically compromised at elevated temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative increase in degradation rates and the critical wear conditions (load, frequency) required to disrupt the oxide film are uncertain and require systematic experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one with the native oxide condition and one where a robust, externally applied protective coating (or engineered oxide) is introduced to minimize galvanic effects. Expose both sets to identical combined wear-corrosion conditions at elevated temperature. Additionally, perform isolated wear and corrosion tests as controls.
measurements: Wear track depth and morphology (via microscopy)
Surface potential mapping (e.g., Scanning Kelvin Probe) to assess galvanic coupling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the engineered protective coating do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in the acceleration of degradation (i.e., if the combined wear-corrosion degradation is not lower than the native oxide samples or does not exceed the additive effects of isolated wear and corrosion), then the proposed micro-galvanic coupling mechanism does not adequately explain the observed accelerated degradation and is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
